/-!
# Oberwolfach problem

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Oberwolfach problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberwolfach_problem)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in
  mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [GJKKO21] Glock, S., Joos, F., Kim, J., Kühn, D., Osthus, D., *Resolution of the Oberwolfach
  problem*, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 23 (2021), 2511–2547.
  [arXiv:1806.04644](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.04644)
- [ABHMS16] Alspach, B., Bryant, D., Horsley, D., Maenhaut, B., Scharaschkin, V., *On
  factorisations of complete graphs into circulant graphs and the Oberwolfach problem*,
  Ars Math. Contemp. 11 (2016), 157–173. [arXiv:1411.6047](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.6047)
- [SDTBD21] Salassa, F., Dragotto, G., Traetta, T., Buratti, M., Della Croce, F., *Merging
  combinatorial design and optimization: the Oberwolfach problem*, Australas. J. Combin. 79 (2021),
  141–166. [arXiv:1903.12112](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.12112)

The Oberwolfach problem, posed by Ringel in 1967, asks which $2$-regular graphs $G$ have the
property that the complete graph $K_n$ on the same number $n$ of vertices can be decomposed into
edge-disjoint copies of $G$. Every $2$-regular graph is a disjoint union of cycles
$C_x + C_y + C_z + \cdots$ (each of length at least $3$), and the instance for this graph is
denoted $OP(x, y, z, \dots)$. A solution can only exist when $n$ is odd, and then it consists of
exactly $(n-1)/2$ copies of $G$.

It is known that $OP(4, 5)$ and $OP(3, 3, 5)$ have no solution. It is widely believed that every
other instance has a solution; this is known for all sufficiently large $n$ [GJKKO21] and for all
$n \le 60$ [SDTBD21].

The problem has also been extended to even $n$: there one asks whether all edges of $K_n$ except
those of a perfect matching can be decomposed into copies of $G$ (necessarily $n/2 - 1$ of them).
Here $OP(3, 3)$ and $OP(3, 3, 3, 3)$ have no solution, and it is widely believed that every other
even instance has one.
-/

blocks.docstring:
A graph `H` on a vertex set `V` *decomposes into copies of* a graph `G` on the same vertex set
if there is a set `D` of graphs on `V`, each isomorphic to `G`, whose edge sets are pairwise
disjoint and whose union is `H`. Equivalently, every edge of `H` lies in exactly one member of `D`.

justification.closest_existing_considered: The ad-hoc indexed pattern in Paper/RingelConjecture.lean (∃ f : Fin k → (V ↪ W), Pairwise edge-disjoint ∧ ⨆ i, T.map (f i) = ⊤); Erdos184.IsDecomposition (Finset of Subgraphs, not restricted to copies of a fixed graph); Mathlib's SimpleGraph.Subgraph.IsPerfectMatching (used for the 1-factor, but Mathlib has no 2-factorisation notion).
justification.name: OberwolfachProblem.DecomposesIntoCopiesOf
justification.why_needed: Neither Mathlib nor FormalConjecturesForMathlib has a notion of a graph decomposition into isomorphic copies (an H-decomposition / 2-factorisation into a given 2-factor). Defined as: ∃ D : Set (SimpleGraph V), (∀ C ∈ D, Nonempty (C ≃g G)) ∧ D.PairwiseDisjoint edgeSet ∧ sSup D = H. Since copies live on the same vertex type as H, they are automatically spanning, and the number of copies ((n-1)/2, resp. n/2-1) is forced by edge counting, so it is not imposed. A provable @[category test] lemma (K_3 decomposes into copies of C_3) exercises the definition. It is kept in the problem file because the task restricts writes to the candidate file; a reviewer may prefer to move it to FormalConjecturesForMathlib/Combinatorics/SimpleGraph/.

blocks.name: DecomposesIntoCopiesOf
blocks.text:
/--
A graph `H` on a vertex set `V` *decomposes into copies of* a graph `G` on the same vertex set
if there is a set `D` of graphs on `V`, each isomorphic to `G`, whose edge sets are pairwise
disjoint and whose union is `H`. Equivalently, every edge of `H` lies in exactly one member of `D`.
-/
def DecomposesIntoCopiesOf (H G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ D : Set (SimpleGraph V),
    (∀ C ∈ D, Nonempty (C ≃g G)) ∧ D.PairwiseDisjoint edgeSet ∧ sSup D = H

@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem top_decomposesIntoCopiesOf_cycleGraph_three :
    DecomposesIntoCopiesOf (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 3)) (cycleGraph 3) := by
  have h : cycleGraph 3 = ⊤ := by ext a b; fin_cases a <;> fin_cases b <;> decide
  exact ⟨{⊤}, by simp [h, Nonempty.intro Iso.refl], Set.pairwiseDisjoint_singleton _ _,
    sSup_singleton⟩

blocks.docstring:
**The Oberwolfach problem** (Ringel, 1967). Let $G$ be a $2$-regular graph on an odd number $n$
of vertices. Then the complete graph $K_n$ on the same vertex set can be decomposed into
edge-disjoint copies of $G$ (necessarily $(n-1)/2$ of them) if and only if $G$ is not one of the
two known exceptions $C_4 + C_5$ (the instance $OP(4, 5)$, $n = 9$) and $C_3 + C_3 + C_5$ (the
instance $OP(3, 3, 5)$, $n = 11$), which are known to have no solution.

The parity restriction is necessary: every vertex of $K_n$ has degree $n - 1$, which must be a
multiple of $2$. The statement is the widely believed answer to Ringel's question of *which*
$2$-regular graphs $G$ admit such a decomposition; it is known for all sufficiently large $n$
[GJKKO21] and for all $n \le 60$ [SDTBD21].

theorem oberwolfach_problem.variants.even [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hG : G.IsRegularOfDegree 2) (hV : Even (Fintype.card V)) :
    (∃ I : (⊤ : SimpleGraph V).Subgraph, I.IsPerfectMatching ∧
      DecomposesIntoCopiesOf (⊤ \ I.spanningCoe) G) ↔

blocks.docstring:
**The Oberwolfach problem for even orders.** Let $G$ be a $2$-regular graph on an even number $n$
of vertices. Then there is a perfect matching $I$ of the complete graph $K_n$ on the same vertex
set such that $K_n - I$ (all edges of $K_n$ except those of $I$) can be decomposed into
edge-disjoint copies of $G$ (necessarily $n/2 - 1$ of them) if and only if $G$ is not one of the
two known exceptions $C_3 + C_3$ (the instance $OP(3, 3)$, $n = 6$) and $C_3 + C_3 + C_3 + C_3$
(the instance $OP(3, 3, 3, 3)$, $n = 12$), which are known to have no solution.

Since every perfect matching of $K_n$ is mapped to every other one by an automorphism of $K_n$,
the existential quantifier over $I$ may equivalently be read as a universal one.

claims.decomposer_note: Open-ended 'which' question, but the article asserts the candidate answer (widely believed): every 2-regular graph G on n vertices (necessarily n odd, since K_n must have even degree; n = 1 has no 2-regular graph) admits a decomposition of K_n into (n-1)/2 edge-disjoint copies of G, except exactly G = C_4 + C_5 (n = 9) and G = C_3 + C_3 + C_5 (n = 11); 'decomposed' means every edge of K_n lies in exactly one copy, and cycles have length >= 3.
claims.reviewer_why: All eight candidates state the same mathematically equivalent iff (for 2-regular G on odd n, K_n decomposes into edge-disjoint copies of G ↔ G ≇ C_4+C_5 and G ≇ C_3+C_3+C_5), which is the widely believed answer prescribed by the table notes; → is the known non-existence for OP(4,5), OP(3,3,5), ← is the open part. c06 chosen for idiomatic Lean: general finite vertex type with [DecidableRel G.Adj] (c01/c02 instead pick up a noncomputable category-theory Fintype instance for LocallyFinite, harmless but unidiomatic), Mathlib cycleGraph/⊕g/≃g for the exceptions, a bespoke set-based decomposition predicate (every edge in exactly one copy; copy count (n-1)/2 is forced by edge counting so not imposed) with a test lemma, and accurate docstrings. Only edit: wrapped an over-long URL line.

claims.decomposer_note: Subordinate even-n extension (K_n minus a 1-factor I, decomposed into n/2 - 1 copies of G) that the article and the cited papers treat as part of OP(F); the article's candidate answer covers it with the exceptions OP(3^2) (n = 6) and OP(3^4) (n = 12) being the only unsolvable even instances, and the existential quantifier over the removed perfect matching is immaterial by symmetry of K_n.
claims.reviewer_why: For 2-regular G on even n: ∃ perfect matching I of K_n (Mathlib Subgraph.IsPerfectMatching on ⊤) with ⊤ \ I.spanningCoe decomposing into edge-disjoint copies of G ↔ G ≇ C_3+C_3 and G ≇ C_3^4, matching the article's exceptions OP(3^2), OP(3^4). The existential over I is the literal reading and immaterial by symmetry (noted in docstring). 'Covered' read as edge-disjoint decomposition per the article's 'exactly once' diner formulation and the cited papers. Boundary n=0 (empty V): both sides true, so no false instance; n=2 vacuous. Same reasons as above for preferring c06's rendering over the equivalent alternatives.

context:
In mathematics, the Oberwolfach problem is an open problem that may be formulated either as a problem of scheduling seating assignments for diners,
or more abstractly as a problem in graph theory, on the edge cycle covers of complete graphs. It is named after the Oberwolfach Research Institute for Mathematics, where the problem was posed in 1967 by Gerhard Ringel. It is known to be true for all sufficiently large complete graphs.

decomposition_objections.text: None. The table's candidate answers (exceptions OP(4,5), OP(3,3,5) for odd n and OP(3^2), OP(3^4) for even n) match the Wikipedia article and the cited papers (Alspach et al. arXiv:1411.6047; Glock et al. arXiv:1806.04644). One remark: the even slot's text span comes from the article body rather than the list entry, so it is a subordinate variant, consistent with the table's description.

namespace OberwolfachProblem

open SimpleGraph

variable {V : Type*}

/--
A graph `H` on a vertex set `V` *decomposes into copies of* a graph `G` on the same vertex set
if there is a set `D` of graphs on `V`, each isomorphic to `G`, whose edge sets are pairwise
disjoint and whose union is `H`. Equivalently, every edge of `H` lies in exactly one member of `D`.
-/
def DecomposesIntoCopiesOf (H G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ D : Set (SimpleGraph V),
    (∀ C ∈ D, Nonempty (C ≃g G)) ∧ D.PairwiseDisjoint edgeSet ∧ sSup D = H

/-- The complete graph on three vertices decomposes into (one) copy of the triangle $C_3$. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem top_decomposesIntoCopiesOf_cycleGraph_three :
    DecomposesIntoCopiesOf (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 3)) (cycleGraph 3) := by
  have h : cycleGraph 3 = ⊤ := by ext a b; fin_cases a <;> fin_cases b <;> decide
  exact ⟨{⊤}, by simp [h, Nonempty.intro Iso.refl], Set.pairwiseDisjoint_singleton _ _,
    sSup_singleton⟩

/--
**The Oberwolfach problem** (Ringel, 1967). Let $G$ be a $2$-regular graph on an odd number $n$
of vertices. Then the complete graph $K_n$ on the same vertex set can be decomposed into
edge-disjoint copies of $G$ (necessarily $(n-1)/2$ of them) if and only if $G$ is not one of the
two known exceptions $C_4 + C_5$ (the instance $OP(4, 5)$, $n = 9$) and $C_3 + C_3 + C_5$ (the
instance $OP(3, 3, 5)$, $n = 11$), which are known to have no solution.

multiple of $2$. The statement is the widely believed answer to Ringel's question of *which*

[GJKKO21] and for all $n \le 60$ [SDTBD21].
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem oberwolfach_problem [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hG : G.IsRegularOfDegree 2) (hV : Odd (Fintype.card V)) :
    DecomposesIntoCopiesOf (⊤ : SimpleGraph V) G ↔
      IsEmpty (G ≃g cycleGraph 4 ⊕g cycleGraph 5) ∧
      IsEmpty (G ≃g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 5) := by
  sorry

/--
**The Oberwolfach problem for even orders.** Let $G$ be a $2$-regular graph on an even number $n$
of vertices. Then there is a perfect matching $I$ of the complete graph $K_n$ on the same vertex
set such that $K_n - I$ (all edges of $K_n$ except those of $I$) can be decomposed into

the existential quantifier over $I$ may equivalently be read as a universal one.

@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem oberwolfach_problem.variants.even [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hG : G.IsRegularOfDegree 2) (hV : Even (Fintype.card V)) :
    (∃ I : (⊤ : SimpleGraph V).Subgraph, I.IsPerfectMatching ∧
      DecomposesIntoCopiesOf (⊤ \ I.spanningCoe) G) ↔
      IsEmpty (G ≃g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3) ∧
      IsEmpty (G ≃g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3 ⊕g cycleGraph 3) := by
  sorry

end OberwolfachProblem

items: The list entry is an open-ended 'which 2-regular graphs' question. Following the decomposition-table notes and the article ('it is widely believed that all other instances have a solution'), it is formalized as the widely believed characterization: an iff between the existence of the decomposition and G not being one of the known exceptions (C_4+C_5, C_3+C_3+C_5 for odd n; C_3+C_3, C_3^4 for even n). An answer(sorry) rendering was considered but rejected: a predicate/set-valued answer over graphs on arbitrary vertex types is awkward and would admit only tautological answers, while the table explicitly asks for the 'except exactly' form. The forward direction (exceptions have no solution) is known; the reverse direction is the open part.

Hypothesis Odd (Fintype.card V) is added to the main slot, as in the article: a decomposition can only exist for odd n (degree parity), so without it the 'all except two exceptions' claim would be false for even n.
The complete graph 'on the same number of vertices' is taken to be ⊤ : SimpleGraph V on G's own vertex type; a 'copy' of G is any graph C on V with Nonempty (C ≃g G), which is automatically spanning.
The number of copies ((n-1)/2, resp. n/2-1) is not imposed; it is forced by edge counting for a 2-regular G, so the statement is equivalent to the literature's phrasing. Docstrings record the count.

Even variant: 'all edges except for a perfect matching can be covered by copies' is read, as in Glock–Joos–Kim–Kühn–Osthus and Alspach et al., as an edge-disjoint decomposition (2-factorisation) of K_n − I. The perfect matching is quantified existentially via Mathlib's Subgraph.IsPerfectMatching on (⊤ : SimpleGraph V) and removed with ⊤ \ I.spanningCoe; by symmetry of K_n this is equivalent to a universal quantifier.
Isomorphism to the exceptional graphs is expressed as IsEmpty (G ≃g cycleGraph a ⊕g cycleGraph b ...) using Mathlib's cycleGraph and disjoint sum ⊕g; #check confirmed the parse G ≃g (… ⊕g …).
[DecidableRel G.Adj] is assumed so that SimpleGraph.IsRegularOfDegree elaborates without global Classical; this imposes no mathematical restriction on G.

Boundary cases: n = 1, 2 are vacuous (no 2-regular graph); n = 3, 4 make both sides true; the degenerate n = 0 case of the even variant (empty graph, empty matching, empty decomposition) makes both sides true and is not excluded.
Vertex type is universe-polymorphic (Type*); Iso to the Fin-based exceptional graphs across universes typechecks.

reviewer_notes: Original statement is an open-ended 'which' question; following the decomposition-table notes and the article, both slots are stated as the widely believed complete characterization (iff form), as in c01–c07. c08's alternative `answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ …, (decomposes ↔ not exceptional)` form has repo precedent (SumOfThreeCubes) and is also faithful, but the direct iff is the more common style for `research open` conjectures and was preferred. No candidate omitted a slot and no objections to the table were raised; I found none either. Verified by compilation/#check: cycleGraph k is C_k (degree-2 for k=3,4,5), `G ≃g A ⊕g B ⊕g C` parses as G ≃g ((A ⊕g B) ⊕g C), IsEdgeColouring/PairwiseDisjoint/sSup encodings are equivalent partitions of the edge set. Small-case sanity: n=3 (C_3, both sides true; test lemma), n=5 (C_5, both true), n=9 with C_4+C_5 (both false), even n=0 (both true). Final file compiles with only the two 'declaration uses sorry' warnings.
